newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia offers A$100,000 extortion reward.
newsitem.headline: Australia offers A$100,000 extortion reward.

text.p: Two Australian state governments on Tuesday offered a combined A$100,000 (US$76,000) reward in the hunt for an extortionist who has threatened to plant poisoned biscuits in supermarkets on Australia's east coast.
The New South Wales and Queensland state governments each approved A$50,000 rewards as the extortionist's Monday deadline passed without incident.
"The joint reward is a $100,000 reward for both governments. Anyone with information relating to that extortion can bring that forward," said New South Wales Police Minister Paul Whelan.
"The significant reward could lead to information that will be of great assistance to both police services in their investigation," Whelan told a news conference.
An extortionist had threatened to plant biscuits laced with a pesticide in supermarkets in both states as from Monday unless four police involved in a 1991 murder case take a lie detector test.
Australia's largest biscuit manufacturer, Arnotts, which received the threat, has removed all its products from stores.
Police have refused to reveal whether there has been any further contact with the extortionist, but have warned shoppers to be vigilant, saying other food companies could be targeted.
Arnotts has stood down a few hundred casual workers, but has warned it was prepared to shut down factory lines and suspend up to 1,000 workers.

Arnotts, which is 70 percent-owned by U.S. food giant Campbell Soup Co, says the extortion crisis will cost it A$5.0 million weekly in lost sales and is working on tamper-proof packaging to get its products back in stores.
Arnotts sells biscuits to Asia, New Zealand and Pacific island countries, but says its exports are safe and that the company's factories and distribution networks are secure.

The extortionist has demanded police involved in a 1991 murder case take a polygraph test in an attempt to prove the innocence of a friend now serving a life sentence for the execution-style murder of a bookmaker.
Police have refused to meet the demand.
"Any form of backdown would be wrong because it would only encourage these creatures," Queensland Police Minister Russell Cooper said on Tuesday.
Police probing the extortion threat have said they want to question John Bobak, for whom there is a A$50,000 reward and a long-standing warrant in place in relation to the 1991 murders.
